newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia stocks mixed as local factors eclipse Dow.
newsitem.headline: Asia stocks mixed as local factors eclipse Dow.

text.p: Asian stock markets were mixed on Tuesday, as Wall Street's record gains overnight propelled some exchanges higher. Others trended lower as a variety of local factors dominated sentiment.
Tokyo stocks roared ahead when trading resumed after Monday's public holiday, with shares gaining more than two percent.
"The strong U.S. markets...influenced the Tokyo markets strongly today," said Haruo Nakaharu, a strategist at Toyo Securities.
"The Nikkei average had some catching up to do since Monday was a holiday in Japan," he added.
Catch up it did. The key Nikkei 225-share average ended 467.95 points or 2.25 percent, higher at 21,310.59.
Wall Street steamed ahead on Monday, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average at one point topping the 5,900 level before ending 51 points up at a record closing high of 5,889.

Expectations that U.S. economic data and moderate inflation would not prompt the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates when its policy makers meet next week spurred the U.S. market ahead by some 179 points last week.

Although many traders remain optimistic that a rise in interest rates will not occur, others still believe the Central Bank could make a preemptive move against inflation and raise rates a modest quarter of a percentage point.
Hong Kong stocks surged to a new 1996 high by the close.
The Hang Seng Index ended up 53.71 points, or 0.46 percent, at 11,621.61, off a peak of 11,645.35. The previous intraday high for the year was 11,600 set in February.

"With precious little news on the domestic front, Hong Kong remains tied to the U.S. interest rate outlook - which now looks limited to a 0.25 percent hike," said James Osborn, sales director at ING Barings.
Wall Street's gains also spurred a sharp rise in Singapore, where the Straits Times Index was up 34.56 points, or 1.60 per cent, at 2,189.05.
"It is the inflow of passive funds triggered off by strong indices like the Dow," said a senior manager from a local brokerage house in Singapore.
Malaysian shares continued to advance aided by revived foreign fund buying and the advances in the Dow, but ended off the day's highs.
"The market's been in hibernation for some time, and now, it's a wake-up call," said an institutional dealer with a foreign firm in Kuala Lumpur.
The key Composite Index closed up 3.33 points, or 0.29 percent, at 1,134.88.
Philippine stocks ended 26.05 points, or 0.81 percent, higher at 3,259.72, while in Indonesia shares gained 7.54 points or 1.36 percent to 561.94.
Elsewhere in Asia, Thai stocks remained pressured by political concerns ahead of a no-confidence debate in parliament against the prime minister which begins on Wednesday.
Thai stocks were off 8.52 points, or 0.80 percent, at 1,050.35.
Stocks in Taiwan eased 40.02 points or 0.61 percent to 6,478.44, nearing a major technical resistance level.
South Korean stocks finished marginally lower at 781.76, off 0.12 points, or 0.02 percent, amid concerns over a large number of margin loans that need to be repaid.
Soft commodities prices pushed Australian stocks lower. The All Ordinaries index ended 13.4 points or 0.59 percent down at 2,254.4.
At 1050 GMT the dollar was at 110.09/0.19 yen and 1.5113/19 marks.
Hong Kong gold bullion ended at US$383.10/60 an ounce against New York's US$383.00/40 close on Monday.
Asian crude prices were lower in the wake of an overnight slump in global crude futures.
SIMEX November Brent futures ended 23 cents higher than London at $21.81 as players decided the selloff was overdone.
